{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=cross-turn+memory+architectures+mechanical+constraints+state+continuity+autonomous+agents&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6323560\", \"title\": [\"SIM: Stateless Intelligence Memory — The Context Continuity Problem in AI Agent Architectures\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p><p>Modern AI agents exhibit sophisticated language understanding, reasoning, and tool-use capabilities. Yet they suffer from a fundamental architectural limitation that prevents them from being reliably deployed in enterprise environments: they cannot maintain coherent context across interactions. We term this the SIM Problem — Stateless Intelligence Memory — and formally define it as the structural inability of an AI agent to maintain, integrate, and reason over accumulated contextual knowledge across sessions, agents, and time. In this paper, we (1) formally define the SIM Problem and its four primary failure modes; (2) present three mathematical theorems establishing the impossibility of resolving SIM through incremental approaches; (3) survey existing approaches — Knowledge Graphs, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, episodic memory, and neurosymbolic systems — and demonstrate through a structured analysis that none satisfies the five necessary conditions for context continuity; and (4) derive these five necessary conditions as a formal specification for any architectural solution. Our analysis is grounded in 44 verified citations spanning cognitive science, knowledge representation, multi-agent systems, and large language model research. Empirical data from enterprise AI deployments confirms that the SIM Problem is not merely theoretical: over 80% of enterprise AI initiatives report no measurable business impact, and Gartner projects that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by 2027. We argue that solving the SIM Problem is the central architectural challenge of the current AI era, and that doing so requires a purpose-built, multi-layer architecture — the specification of which we leave to a forthcoming companion paper.</p></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6323560\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1049/ic:20050177\", \"title\":…

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=intrinsic+motivation+metrics+benchmark+goal+generation+autonomous+agents&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202607.0905.v1\", \"title\": [\"Beyond Human-Designed Objectives: Autonomous Goal Generation in AI Through Intrinsic Motivation and Self-Directed Agency\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Current artificial intelligence systems remain fundamentally constrained by their dependence on human-designed objectives and reward functions, limiting their capacity for genuine autonomy and open-ended development. This paper proposes Autonomous Goal Generation Networks (AGGNs), a theoretical framework for architectures that synthesize, evaluate, and pursue their own objectives through intrinsic motivation. The framework specifies five components: Goal-Generative Networks (GGNs, based on a VAE-style sampler over a goal embedding space), Objective Evaluation Systems (OESs) with six explicit criteria, Intrinsic Motivation Engines (IMEs) implementing curiosity, competence, empowerment, autonomy, and aesthetic drives, Autonomous Agency Controllers (AACs) for concurrent-objective scheduling, and Self-Reflective Goal Refinement (SRGR) for closing the loop. We prove a goal-distribution convergence result (Theorem 1) under stationary feedback and a stability condition for the SRGR loop. The contribution of this paper is theoretical: we identify the structural and motivational ingredients an autonomously-goal-generating agent must possess. No empirical validation is reported. Section VI specifies the protocol — benchmarks (Minecraft-like exploration, creative reasoning, robotic skill acquisition, scientific discovery, multi-agent social tasks), baselines (curiosity-driven exploration, empowerment maximization, novelty search), and metrics (goal diversity, coherence, achievement rate, exploration efficiency) — against which AGGNs should be evaluated.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0905.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 7, 14]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1609/aaai.v32i1.12195\", \"title\": [\"Adversarial Goal Generation for Intrinsic Motivation\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>\\n      \\n        Generally in Reinforcement Learning the goal, or reward sign…

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=automated+reasoning+model+safety+failure+profiles+self+correction+limitations&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6991012\", \"title\": [\"Automated Oversight Diagnostic Self-Correction and Failure-Aware Reasoning for GUI Agents(ChinaMM)\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The rapid evolution of Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) has significantly advanced autonomous GUI agents. However, during the development of GUI agents for dynamic scenarios, error compounding leads to a labor-intensive and expensive bottleneck, requiring high costs for manual intervention. Meanwhile, errors are hard to be located and difficult to track failure reasoning. Consequently, it is challenging to overcome random errors simply by blindly increasing the size of the training dataset and address errors in a targeted manner. Existing research primarily attempt to improve GUI agent by optimizing the agent&apos;s internal design to avoid outcome deviation, ignoring the critical need for automated self-correction in step-level agent errors. In view of this, we propose the Automated Oversight (AO), an efficient four-stage closed-loop approach designed to emulate human-level oversight. The architecture consists of four key phases: (1) global outcome verification for final-state checking; (2) step-level visual trajectory alignment to intercept errors in real-time; (3) teacher-driven root-cause diagnosis to analyze failures; and (4) closed-loop rectification with state rollback to recover the task. Unlike traditional methods, AO focuses on failure-aware reasoning to identify the root causes of errors and execute targeted recovery. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method can improve agent success rates and reduce human cognitive burden by achieving reliable autonomous interactions in dynamic systems. We will publicly release our code.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6991012\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1023/a:1006143621319\", \"title\": [\"Autarky Pruning in Propositional Model Elimination Reduces Failure Redundancy\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1006143621319\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[1999, 8]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.100…
